articles.title: CYP24A1 rs1570669 and rs2762934 polymorphisms and bladder cancer susceptibility: a Turkish case-control study.
articles.abstract: Bladder cancer (BC) is one of the most common malignant tumours of the urinary system and represents an important public health problem. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are common human genetic variations and may affect cancer risk by altering various genetic processes such as vitamin D metabolism and tumour suppression. CYP24A1 rs1570669 and rs2762934 polymorphisms may be relevant to cancer biology through their potential effects on the degradation of active vitamin D metabolites. These polymorphisms have been associated with the risk of urinary cancer, including BC, in an Asian population. To the best of our knowledge, the impact of CYP24A1 rs2762934 and rs1570669 variants on BC susceptibility has not yet been investigated in any Caucasian cohort. Consequently, this study represents the first attempt to evaluate their associations with BC risk within a Turkish population. The present study investigated CYP24A1 gene polymorphisms in 152 BC patients and 178 healthy controls using a TaqMan allelic discrimination assay with real-time PCR (qPCR). Neither polymorphism was significantly associated with BC risk, although the A alleles of both variants showed a non-significant trend towards increased odds of BC. Additionally, both groups differed significantly regarding age, BMI, and smoking status, but not regarding other characteristics, such as vitamin D levels. The CYP24A1 rs2762934 and rs1570669 polymorphisms were not significantly associated with BC susceptibility in this Turkish cohort. Despite this, the A alleles of both variants showed a non-significant trend toward increased odds of BC, which may warrant further investigation in larger cohorts.

articles.title: Purine and citrate metabolism in urolithiasis and bladder cancer: An integrated genetic, gene-expression, and targeted metabolite analysis.
articles.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of bladder cancer (BC), but the contribution of inherited variation in purine and citrate metabolism remains incompletely understood. Because urolithiasis shares selected metabolic and epidemiological features with BC, we compared both disorders to identify shared and disease-specific molecular patterns. We analysed polymorphisms in ACLY, XDH, PNP, HPRT1, and GART together with targeted gene expression in peripheral blood-derived RNA and urinary citrate, hypoxanthine, and glycine measured by <sup>1</sup>H NMR in a Polish case-control cohort. Genetic associations were assessed using multivariable models adjusted for age, sex, smoking, and BMI, with BH-FDR correction. Genotype-expression, genotype-metabolite, and expression-metabolite relationships were evaluated, and peripheral findings were compared with GSE13507 and TCGA-BLCA bladder-tissue data. ACLY rs2304497 was associated with both diseases, whereas PNP rs1713420 showed a BC-specific association after multivariable adjustment and BH-FDR correction. XDH rs2295475 associations did not remain significant after multiple-testing correction, and formal interaction analyses provided no BH-FDR-significant evidence of effect modification. Peripheral ACLY and GART transcript abundance was lower in both disease groups, while PNP was additionally lower in urolithiasis. Urinary citrate and hypoxanthine were reduced only in urolithiasis. No cross-layer associations remained significant after adjustment and BH-FDR correction. In external bladder tissue, GART was increased in both datasets, while ACLY and HPRT1 were increased in paired TCGA-BLCA tumours. The findings indicate shared and disease-specific molecular patterns but do not support a simple linear relationship between inherited variation, peripheral transcript abundance, and urinary metabolites. Direct functional and tissue-specific validation is required.

articles.title: Consumption of Processed Meat and Unprocessed Red Meat and Risk of Bladder Cancer: A Pooled Analysis of 30 Cohort Studies.
articles.abstract: Background: Processed meat and unprocessed red meat are considered carcinogenic and 'probably carcinogenic' to humans, respectively, but findings for bladder cancer remain inconsistent. Objectives: We assessed associations between processed meat and unprocessed red meat intake and bladder cancer risk using data from the Pooling Project of Prospective Studies of Diet and Cancer. Methods: Associations with bladder cancer risk were assessed using individual-level data from 30 cohort studies from North America, Europe, Australia and Asia. Diet was assessed at enrolment using validated food frequency questionnaires or diet histories. Following a pre-specified analysis plan, study- and sex-specific hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using Cox regression, adjusted for smoking status and duration and other potential confounders, and pooled using inverse-variance-weighted random-effects meta-analysis. Results: During median follow-up across cohorts of 8-29 years, among 2,575,971 participants, 20,780 were diagnosed with bladder cancer. Processed meat intake was associated with increased bladder cancer risk (HR comparing ≥40 with <5 g/day = 1.08; 95% CI: 1.02-1.15; HR per 20 g/day = 1.02; 95% CI: 1.00-1.03). Weaker evidence of association with increased risk was also observed for unprocessed red meat (HR comparing ≥100 with <20 g/day = 1.06; 95% CI: 1.00-1.13; HR per 50 g/day = 1.01; 95% CI: 0.99-1.03). There was no evidence of heterogeneity by study, sex, or region. Conclusions: Higher intakes of processed meat and unprocessed red meat were associated with a small increase in risk of bladder cancer. These findings are consistent with existing public health recommendations to limit consumption of red and processed meat.

articles.title: Navigating the landscape of targeted therapies for renal cell carcinoma in the era of precision medicine (Review).
articles.abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is a biologically heterogeneous malignancy characterized by dysregulation of angiogenic signaling, immune evasion and epigenetic remodeling. Advances in molecular profiling have redefined RCC as a pathway‑driven disease, enabling the development of targeted therapies and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) that have notably improved clinical outcomes. The present review evaluated current evidence on the molecular basis and therapeutic landscape of RCC, with emphasis on von Hippel‑Lindau‑hypoxia‑inducible factor signaling, chromatin remodeling alterations and immune regulatory pathways. The present review summarizes pivotal phase III clinical trials evaluating VEGF‑targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors, mechanistic target of rapamycin inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitors and combination regimens, including nivolumab plus ipilimumab, pembrolizumab + axitinib and lenvatinib + pembrolizumab. Emerging biomarkers, including International Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Database Consortium risk stratification, programmed death‑ligand 1 expression and chromatin remodeling gene alterations (polybromo 1/BRG1‑associated factor 180, BRCA1‑associated protein 1 and SET domain containing 2), are discussed in the context of their clinical utility and limitations. Despite marked progress, durable predictive biomarkers and optimal treatment sequencing strategies remain unresolved. Resistance to therapy emerges through adaptive angiogenic signaling, immune escape and metabolic reprogramming, underscoring the need for integrated multi‑omics approaches and rational combination strategies. By integrating molecular biology with clinical trial evidence, the present review provides a structured framework for understanding therapeutic decision‑making in RCC and highlights future directions toward biomarker‑guided precision oncology.

articles.title: Development and validation of a ferroptosis and metabolic reprogramming gene signature for risk stratification in bladder urothelial carcinoma: A retrospective multicohort study.
articles.abstract: Bladder urothelial carcinoma (BLCA) is clinically and molecularly heterogeneous, and conventional clinicopathologic factors do not fully reflect the biological variation associated with survival. We aimed to develop and externally evaluate a prognostic signature based on genes related to both ferroptosis and metabolic reprogramming and to examine its clinical and biological associations. The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-BLCA transcriptomic and clinical data were used for candidate-gene identification and model development. A 10-gene least absolute shrinkage and selection operator Cox signature was evaluated by complete-pipeline bootstrap validation. After platform harmonization, the same coefficients and TCGA-derived cutoff were applied to GSE13507 and GSE48075. Clinical adjustment, stage-specific analyses, immune analyses accounting for the IFNG score contribution, tumor purity, and molecular subtype, exploratory drug-response prediction, and expression analysis in 15 paired institutional tumor and adjacent tissues were performed. The signature comprised JUN, IFNG, CAV1, SREBF1, G6PD, TFRC, SCD, ZEB1, SLC7A11, and WWTR1. In TCGA-BLCA (401 patients; 176 deaths), the high-risk group had poorer overall survival (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.313; 95% confidence interval = 1.697-3.154; P < .001). The fixed TCGA cutoff also identified high-risk groups in GSE13507 (165 patients; 69 deaths; HR = 2.202; P = .0010) and GSE48075 (73 patients; 45 deaths; HR = 2.476; P = .0082). The 10-gene RiskScore yielded 1-, 3-, and 5-year areas under the curve of 0.644, 0.657, and 0.668 in TCGA-BLCA; the corresponding values ranged from 0.583 to 0.696 in the external cohorts. RiskScore remained associated with survival after adjustment for age, sex, and stage in TCGA (HR per standard-deviation increase, 1.573; P < .001). In the paired institutional cohort, 5 genes differed between tumor and adjacent tissues at a false discovery rate below 0.05, and 9 of 10 genes showed expression directions concordant with TCGA. Enrichment analyses highlighted oxidative-stress and metabolic pathways; several immune and checkpoint associations remained after sensitivity analyses, and exploratory modeling identified risk-group differences in predicted drug sensitivity. The 10-gene signature consistently stratified overall survival across TCGA-BLCA and 2 independent Gene Expression Omnibus cohorts. Its associations with clinical outcome, paired-tissue expression, and immune features support further investigation of ferroptosis-related metabolic heterogeneity in BLCA.
